front: A plot of sound level in dB against the logarithm of $I/I_0$ is a straight line with slope {{c1::10}}.
why: dB semi-log slope is graph trivia; the definition card covers it

front: A siren and a listener move at the same velocity in the same direction; the observed frequency is {{c1::unchanged}}.
why: No relative motion means no Doppler shift; edge case of the Doppler card

front: A sound is 10 times more intense than another. How many decibels louder, and does it sound ten times as loud?
why: 10x intensity = +10 dB; standard decibel reasoning

front: Acoustic impedance is {{c1::$Z = \rho v$}}, and reflection at a boundary is strongest when {{c1::the mismatch is large}}.
why: Acoustic impedance Z=rho*v is prep-book ultrasound detail beyond the outline

front: Describe the Doppler effect.
why: Doppler effect direction; on essentially every administration

front: How do you reason out the direction of a Doppler shift without the formula?
why: Doppler direction reasoning; restates the Doppler card

front: How does sound intensity vary with distance from a point source?
why: Inverse-square intensity from a point source; common calculation

front: In Doppler ultrasound of blood flow, why does the angle between beam and vessel matter?
why: Doppler beam angle cos(theta) is off-outline ultrasound detail

front: Raising sound intensity by a factor of 1000 raises the level by {{c1::30 dB}}.
why: Factor 1000 intensity = +30 dB; standard decibel arithmetic

front: Sound intensity is proportional to {{c1::amplitude squared}}, so doubling the amplitude multiplies intensity by {{c1::4}}.
why: Intensity proportional to amplitude squared; common wave-property item

front: Sound level in decibels is {{c1::$\beta = 10\log(I/I_0)$}}.
why: Decibel definition beta=10log(I/I0); calculated every year

front: The threshold of hearing is {{c1::$10^{-12}$ W/m$^2$}}, defined as {{c1::0 dB}}.
why: Threshold of hearing 1e-12 W/m^2 = 0 dB; reference value used in dB problems

front: Ultrasound imaging relies on:
why: Ultrasound relies on impedance reflection; passage context

front: Why do higher-frequency ultrasound probes give better resolution but shallower penetration?
why: Ultrasound resolution vs penetration tradeoff is off-outline

front: Why is coupling gel applied between an ultrasound transducer and the skin?
why: Coupling gel impedance matching is ultrasound trivia

front: A vibrating surface pushing outward creates a {{c1::compression}} in the air; pulling back leaves a {{c2::rarefaction}}.
why: Sound-production vocabulary supports passage reading more than calculation.

front: Why does a wind instrument go sharp as it warms up during a concert?
why: The 'decide what is fixed' reasoning is a passage favorite.

front: Two identical $70$ dB alarms sound together. The combined level is about {{c1::$73$ dB}}.
why: Decibel arithmetic is tested on nearly every MCAT.

front: A sound becomes $5$ times as intense. About how much does its level rise?
why: Non-power-of-ten ratios test the +3 dB rule directly.

front: A blender delivers $10^{-5}$ W/m$^2$ to your ear. What is the sound level?
why: Converting intensity to decibels is a standard discrete question.

front: A loudspeaker produces $90$ dB at $1$ m. Treating it as a point source and ignoring absorption, what is the level at $10$ m?
why: Inverse-square spreading combined with decibels is frequently tested.

front: Why does distant thunder sound like a low rumble while nearby thunder is a sharp crack?
why: Frequency-dependent attenuation is mostly passage context.

front: A violin and a flute play the same note. Why do they sound different?
why: Mapping physical properties to pitch, loudness and timbre is commonly tested.

front: Human hearing spans about {{c1::20 Hz to 20 kHz}}; sound below that range is called {{c2::infrasound}}.
why: Hearing range and the definitions of infrasound and ultrasound are commonly tested.

front: In $f' = f\,(v \pm v_o)/(v \mp v_s)$, how do you choose each sign?
why: Doppler direction and sign choice are tested on nearly every MCAT.

front: A $600$ Hz siren approaching a still listener at $34$ m/s is heard at about $667$ Hz ($v = 340$ m/s). A listener running at $34$ m/s toward a parked siren hears {{c1::$660$ Hz}}.
why: Distinguishing moving-observer and moving-source cases is commonly tested.

front: Sound reflecting off a target moving at speed $u$ (much slower than sound) has its frequency shifted by about {{c1::$2fu/v$}}.
why: The reflection double shift underlies Doppler ultrasound questions.

front: An ultrasound echo returns $130\;\mu\text{s}$ after the pulse leaves the probe ($v = 1540$ m/s in tissue). How deep is the reflecting boundary?
why: Echo-depth calculation is a standard ultrasound question.

front: An ultrasound probe's crystal is {{c1::piezoelectric}}: it deforms when a voltage is applied and generates a voltage when squeezed.
why: The transducer mechanism appears in imaging passages.

front: With the same probe and beam angle, the Doppler shift inside a stenosis is $3$ times the upstream shift. The lumen's area there is {{c1::one-third}} of the upstream area.
why: Doppler blood flow paired with continuity is a common combined passage question.

front: A jet flies level at Mach $1.5$. When does a listener on the ground hear its sonic boom?
why: Shock waves are tested qualitatively, mostly in passages.

front: A Mach cone's half-angle satisfies {{c1::$\sin\theta = 1/M$}}, so a faster source makes a narrower cone.
why: Inside the lesson's low-yield block; the cone-angle formula is rarely tested.
